tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NeurIPS 2020 paper (arXiv 2010.01709) reports a 4.5x geometric-mean speedup of AD on optimized IR over AD before optimization and benchmark-by-benchmark comparisons against Tapenade and Adept on a quiesced AWS c4.8xlarge; no compiler flags or public benchmark code path stated, so not A.

corrections.caveats: NeurIPS 2020 paper; compiler versions/flags not stated and benchmark code location not given in the paper. The headline 4.5x is Enzyme vs its own AD on unoptimized IR; vs Tapenade and Adept the paper gives per-benchmark results only, no single ratio. Baselines are AD tools, not ML kernels. License: Apache-2.0 with LLVM Exceptions (LICENSE file).

notes: License identified from the LICENSE file (Apache v2.0 with LLVM Exceptions), so usability moves to copyable. GitHub commits page is blocked by robots.txt, so last_commit (2026-10-01) could not be checked and is left as is.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NeurIPS 2024 paper benchmarks FA3 against cuDNN attention on H100 SXM5: FP16 up to 740 TFLOPs/s and faster than cuDNN for sequence lengths >= 1k; FP8 is behind cuDNN for hdim 128/256 with causal masking. The benchmark script path was not confirmed, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: FP16 forward up to 740 TFLOPs/s (75% utilization), 1.5-2.0x faster than FlashAttention-2 in the forward pass; outperforms cuDNN for medium/long sequences (>= 1k); FP8 reaches close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s and is competitive with cuDNN, but behind it for hdim 128/256 with causal masking. No single speedup ratio vs cuDNN read.
corrections.caveats: NeurIPS 2024 paper; benchmark script location in repo (benchmarks/, hopper/) not confirmed, so tier B not A. Not uniformly faster than cuDNN (FP8 causal hdim128/256 lags). The 'up to 1.5x vs cuDNN' figure in the original record was not found on the pages read. Toolchain versions differ between paper versions (v2: CUDA 12.2, cuDNN 9.0.0, CUTLASS 3.3). cuDNN has since added its own FA-style kernels, so the gap may have narrowed.

notes: arXiv v2 states CUDA 12.2 / cuDNN 9.0.0 / CUTLASS 3.3 at 1830 MHz; the record's CUDA 12.3 / cuDNN 9.1.1.17 / CUTLASS 3.5 may come from v3, which I could not open (HTTP 429), so compiler_and_flags is left uncorrected. The commits page is blocked by robots.txt, so last_commit was not checked.

tier_reason: Intel-authored arXiv paper (first-party) Table 3 gives next-token latency vs a ggml-based solution on 4th Gen Xeon, with no compiler/flags, exact CPU model or benchmark code path; C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper Table 3: GPT-J 6B 19.98 ms (LLM Runtime, group size 128) vs 31.62 ms (ggml-based, group size 32); the 1.6x headline compares LLM Runtime gs128 to ggml gs32. At equal group size 32: 22.99 vs 31.62 ms, ~1.38x (derived from page data); Llama-2 7B 23.4 vs 27.71 ms, GPT-NeoX 20B 80.16 vs 92.36 ms. README claims up to 40x vs llama.cpp (not verified).
corrections.caveats: Repo archived 2024-08-30; Intel no longer maintains it (README points to Intel Extension for PyTorch). Paper code link is intel-extension-for-transformers. First-party Intel numbers; compiler flags and exact CPU SKU not stated. The 1.6x headline mixes group sizes (LLM Runtime gs128 vs ggml gs32); like-for-like gs32 gains are ~1.2-1.4x. Baseline llama.cpp/ggml is not a listed incumbent.

notes: Metadata matches (Apache-2.0, 352 stars, archived 2024-08-30). The 1.6x headline compares different quantization group sizes, which is worth recording as a shortcoming.
